title: GPU hot-pool eviction stressrun — personal bench notes (Liam)
content:
Purpose:
Quick exploratory stress run to understand how the GPU hot-pool eviction policy affects tail latency and request drop behavior under sudden multi-tenant burst traffic. This is a personal scratchpad — notes, raw numbers, and hypotheses. Not polished.

Environment:
- Cluster: dev-gpu-cluster-3 (4x A100 80GB per node)
- Runtime: serving-runtime:v2.19.0-experimental
- Hot-pool config: size=6 (concurrent model instances), eviction_policy=LRU+age, reserved_idle_secs=30
- Routing: weighted-random across 3 model variants (base, quantized-8, fast-medium)
- Workload driver: in-house qps-flood v0.4 (HTTP/1.1), 256B prompt, no streaming
- Observability hooks: token-level tracing OFF, latency histograms bucketed at ms resolution

Test plan (3 runs):
1) Baseline ramp: linear 0 -> 800 qps over 120s, hold 60s, ramp down.
2) Microburst: hold 200 qps, then 2s spike to 2200 qps, repeat every 45s for 8 cycles.
3) Sustained overload: step to 1100 qps for 300s then reduce to 400 qps.

Metrics captured:
- effective QPS served (requests/s)
- p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms) from gateway perspective
- GPU utilization per node
- eviction_count and cold-start_count (runtime counters)
- request_drop_count (gateway rejects)

Run 1 (baseline):
- nominal QPS achieved: 780 ± 12 rps
- p50: 18 ms, p90: 42 ms, p95: 58 ms, p99: 120 ms
- eviction_count: 2 (single evictions during ramp), cold-start_count: 2
- notes: smooth; warm-cache steady after 90s. No meaningful request drops.

Run 2 (microburst):
Summary timeline (representative cycle):
- pre-spike steady @200 rps for 20s -> p99 ~ 95 ms
- spike 0–2s to 2200 rps: gateway accepted ~1400 rps in first 2s, then started queuing/backpressure
- observed behavior:
  - immediate p99 spike to 1400–2200 ms during first 5s of spike window
  - eviction_count increased by 18 across nodes over first two cycles
  - cold-start_count rose by 12 (many model instances spun up, then expired)
  - request_drop_count: small but visible: ~3.6% of attempted requests returned 503 during high tail
  - GPU util: saturated at 98–100% on primary nodes, secondary nodes hit 80–95% as instances moved
- after spike (10–15s): p99 slowly returned to ~110 ms as caches refill

Quick ascii latency sketch (p99) by time in a single cycle:
[ before spike ] -----95ms----- |SPIKE--> ###### 1400ms #### | cooldown ---110ms---

Interpretation:
- Hot-pool size=6 is too small to absorb a 2s 10x spike when routing attempts to create additional instances; eviction churn causes additional cold-starts which amplifies tail.
- LRU+age eviction works in steady state but not for aggressive bursts since newer, warm instances get evicted when the system tries to reassign capacity.
- Gateway backpressure mitigates some throughput but still leads to 503s under the highest instantaneous arrival rate.

Run 3 (sustained overload):
- target 1100 rps sustained for 300s
- nominal achieved: 1075 ± 35 rps
- p50: 23 ms, p90: 78 ms, p95: 130 ms, p99: 410 ms (sustained tail elevation)
- eviction_count steady ~4 evictions per minute, cold-start_count ~1 every 90s
- request_drop_count ~0.7% (gateway kept most requests but with increased queuing)
- notes: unlike microbursts, system reaches a new steady degraded tail but fewer cold-starts because hot-pool resized implicitly by autoscaler (took ~45s to add node capacity).

Raw numbers table (selected):
- baseline p99: 120 ms
- microburst peak p99: 1.6s (avg across cycles)
- microburst request drops: 3.6% attempts
- sustained p99: 410 ms

Hypotheses and root cause sketch:
1) Eviction-churn loop: when ephemeral bursts force instance creation, eviction policy removes warm instances that are likely to be reused in the immediate cooldown window. When load subsides, those evicted instances must cold-start again => extra tail.
2) Autoscaler reaction time critical: if autoscaler can add node capacity in <20s, sustained overload can be handled with fewer cold starts. Our autoscale is ~45s here.
3) Gateway smoothing: gateway accepts bursts up to a point but aggressive acceptance without shaping leads to queue build and timeouts; a softer admission controller could reduce p99 spikes at the cost of higher immediate 503s (trade).

Experiments to run next (priority order):
- A) Hot-pool policy: test MRU-biased eviction (prefer evicting older/warmest less likely to be hot) and TTL-based grace (extend reserved_idle_secs to 90s) to see if microburst tail reduces.
- B) Admission shaping: run microburst but cap accept-rate to 1200 rps at gateway for 3s window and measure p99 vs 503 tradeoff.
- C) Autoscaler tuning: set scale cooldown to 10s and target-utilization threshold lower, re-run sustained overload.
- D) Warm-reuse: attempt a pre-warm pool for top-3 models with pinned instances that do not get evicted during bursts.

Quick heuristics from this run (for ops notes):
- If customer workload shows frequent 1–3s spikes > 3x baseline, advise increasing hot-pool by at least 2x and enabling longer reserved_idle_secs.
- For latency-sensitive real-time apps, prefer admission shaping over blind acceptance — lower p99 is more user-visible than a few percent 503s.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Is eviction_count correlated more strongly with model size or with request concurrency? Need per-model breakdown.
- Can we capture a timeline-flame (eviction vs cold-start events) mapped to request ids? That will make root-cause definitive.
- Validate whether MRU-eviction or TTL-grace has the biggest ROI (latency reduction per extra GPU-hour).

Notes to self:
- Push a small instrumentation PR to emit eviction_reason tag on tracing spans (PR linked above).
- Re-run microburst with longer trace window once reason tag merged.
- Check if Quantized instances have faster cold-starts (lower p99 amplification) — quick A/B later.

End of scratchpad.

-- Liam
